title: Classes and Objects
description: Create your own kind of thing with a class, then make objects from it.

content.real: A cookie cutter and its cookies
content.text: Tracking three dogs with plain variables gets messy fast. A **class** is the cookie cutter: you describe the data and the actions once. Each **object** is a cookie stamped from it: same shape, but its own cookie.

items.sub: Describes a whole kind of thing, in one place.
Data stored on each object, like a name and a breed.
One real thing made from the class. Make as many as you want.

content.question: In the cookie cutter picture, what is the object?
content.explain: The cutter is the class (the blueprint). Each cookie stamped out of it is an object.

items: Start with the `class` keyword and a name.
By convention the name starts with a capital letter: `Dog`, not `dog`.
Inside goes a special method called `__init__`.
Python runs `__init__` **automatically** every time a new object is made.
Its job: store that object's own data.
content.title: How a class starts

content.caption: This only defines the blueprint, so nothing prints yet.

parts.label: this object
parts.note: `self` means this particular object, the one being built right now.

parts.label: attribute
parts.note: A value stored on an object is called an **attribute**.

parts.label: value passed in
parts.note: The name that was handed to `Dog(...)` when the object was made.

content.title: Anatomy of an attribute line
content.caption: Read it as: take the name that was passed in, and store it on this object.

content.value: Every method inside a class takes `self` as its first parameter, and Python fills it in for you. You never pass it yourself: you write `buddy.bark()`, not `buddy.bark(buddy)`.
content.title: self is automatic

content.question: What does `self` mean inside a method?
options: The first argument you type yourself
The object the method is working on right now
content.explain: `self` is this particular object. Python passes it in for you, so each object works with its own data.

items: A function written inside a class is called a **method**.
Methods are how a class **does** things.
Because a method gets `self`, it can reach the attributes of whichever object called it.
content.title: Methods

content.caption: Two methods added: `bark` and `describe`. Still just the blueprint, so nothing prints yet.

items.title: Attributes (what it knows)
items.text: Values stored on each object. No parentheses.

items.title: Methods (what it does)
items.text: Functions inside the class. You call them with parentheses.

content.question: What is a function written inside a class called?
content.explain: Functions that live inside a class are called methods. Values stored on an object are attributes.

items: Write the class name with parentheses: `Dog(...)`.
Pass in the values `__init__` expects (but not `self`).
Each object is completely separate, with its own attributes.
Use a dot to reach an attribute (`dog1.name`) or call a method (`dog2.bark()`).
content.title: Building an object

steps.note: Python reads the whole class and remembers the blueprint. No object exists yet.
`Dog("Buddy", "Pug")` asks for a new object. Python makes an empty one and runs `__init__` on it.
`self` is the new, empty object. `name` and `breed` hold the values you passed in.
Store the name on this object as an attribute.
Store the breed too. `__init__` is done.
The finished object is stored in `dog1`. The temporary `name` and `breed` are gone, but the attributes stay on the object.
Call `bark` on `dog1`. Python passes `dog1` in as `self` for you.

content.title: Watch an object being built
content.outro: `__init__` ran automatically and stored the data. `bark` used `self` to find that data.

content.question: After `dog1 = Dog("Buddy", "Pug")`, what is `dog1.breed`?
content.explain: `__init__` stored the second value, `"Pug"`, as `self.breed`, and `self` was `dog1`.

content.title: Two cookies, one cutter
content.caption: Same class, but each object keeps its own attributes.

content.question: Using the `Dog` class above, what does this print?
content.explain: `bark` was called on `pet`, so `self` is `pet` and `self.name` is `"Rex"`.

content.value: Change the names in the two cards below and press the buttons. The method is written once, so both cards share it, and yet each one prints its own line. That is `self` doing its job.

editorCode:
class Cat:
    def __init__(self, name, color):
        self.name = name
        self.color = color

    def meow(self):
        print(self.name + " says Meow!")

cat1 = Cat("Luna", "black")
cat2 = Cat("Sky", "grey")

cat1.meow()
cat2.meow()
print(cat2.color)

quiz.question: What is a class in Python?
quiz.explain: A class describes a kind of thing. One class can stamp out as many separate objects as you need.

quiz.question: What does 'self' mean inside a method?
options: This particular object, the one the method was called on
quiz.explain: self is how a method reaches the attributes of whichever object it was called on, which is why one method can print a different name for every object.

quiz.question: Which method runs automatically when you make a new object?
quiz.explain: __init__ runs the moment an object is created, and its job is to store that object's own starting values.
